nameStory: The Conical Trashline Orbweaver gets its name from two distinctive features: the cone-shaped bump on its abdomen and its habit of decorating its web with a 'trashline' of debris. This vertical stripe of dead insects, leaves, and other bits creates what looks like nature's version of a junk drawer hanging right in the middle of an otherwise pristine orb web.
description: This tiny spider is a master of disguise, measuring only about the size of a pencil eraser when fully grown. Females reach up to 7.5mm while males are even smaller at around 4mm. What makes this orbweaver special isn't its size, but its clever decorating habits—it strings together dead prey and debris in a vertical line through the center of its circular web, then hides among the 'trash' where its mottled brown coloration makes it nearly invisible.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for a classic orb web with a distinctive vertical stripe of debris running down the center—dead insects, plant bits, and other 'trash' strung together like beads on a necklace

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: The spider sits motionless on its trashline, perfectly camouflaged among the debris; when disturbed, it plays dead rather than fleeing

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Quite small—females about the size of a pencil eraser (5-8mm), males even tinier at 3-4mm; easy to overlook without the telltale web decoration

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen with mottled brown and gray coloring that feels rough-textured; the cone-shaped bump gives it an angular silhouette

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Cryptic brown, gray, and sometimes yellowish patterns that perfectly mimic dead plant material and dried insects

habitat: Found in gardens, forest edges, and shrublands throughout New England, typically spinning webs between low branches, garden plants, or tall grasses. They prefer spots with plenty of flying insects and natural debris to incorporate into their web decorations. Look for them in areas where leaf litter and small twigs are readily available for their camouflage collections.

seasonality.spring: Young spiders emerge and begin building their first webs, though trashlines may be sparse as they're still learning their craft.
seasonality.summer: Peak web-building season when mature females create elaborate trashline decorations and are most easily spotted in gardens and forest edges.
seasonality.fall: Adults are at their largest and most visible, with impressive debris collections in their webs before mating and egg-laying activities begin.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off after laying eggs, leaving only egg sacs hidden in protected spots to survive until spring.

funFact: This spider is such a convincing mimic that even when it's sitting right in the open on its web, most people mistake it for just another piece of dead debris—until it suddenly moves, creating a startling 'magic trick' moment that often makes observers jump!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Humped Trashline Orbweaver, but the Conical has a more pointed, cone-like bump on its abdomen versus the Humped's rounded hump. Memory trick: 'Conical' sounds like 'cone'—look for the pointier silhouette.
compareHints: The Conical Trashline Orbweaver differs from its close relative, the Humped Trashline Orbweaver, primarily in the shape of its abdominal projection—conical and pointed rather than rounded and humped. Both species create similar debris-decorated webs, but the Conical tends to be slightly smaller and its body shape more angular overall. The web decorations and hiding behavior are nearly identical between the two species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its closest relative, the Conical Trashline Orbweaver, the Humped species has a distinctly rounded abdominal projection rather than a sharp, pointed one.
